title: You take yourself along
hookLine: travel won't cure discontent, because you take yourself with you (Letters 28)
last: CALVISIUS SABINUS — NOBODY CAN LEARN IT FOR ME.

lines: SCROLLING FLIGHTS ON A GRAY WEDNESDAY.
THE WORRY HAD A TICKET TOO.
LUCILIUS TRAVELS, AND IT DOESN'T WORK.
cards: It's three in the afternoon on a gray Wednesday and you're scrolling flights. Somewhere warm, with a different language and a different you, the one who's relaxed, reads novels and doesn't check email. Maybe you even go.
And on the third night, in the lovely room by the sea, the same old worry turns up, like it had a ticket too. Lucilius has been traveling, hoping to shake off a heaviness he can't name.
In the twenty-eighth letter, Seneca says he's not surprised it didn't work, and explains why in one sentence.

teach.h: CHANGE YOUR SOUL, NOT YOUR SKY.
teach.b: Do you think you're the only one, Seneca asks, who has found that long trips and changes of scenery don't shake off sadness? You need to change your soul, not your sky. In Latin: animum debes mutare, non caelum.

Then he passes on a reply attributed to Socrates, to someone who complained that travel did him no good: why are you surprised, when you take yourself along? The same cause that drove you out goes with you.
Seneca's picture is cargo: a heavy load, badly stowed. Every lurch of the ship makes it worse. Run from place to place and you shake the load around.
Set it down and the journey becomes a pleasure. He's not against travel.

teach.h: THE WHOLE WORLD IS MY HOMELAND.
teach.b: Once the soul is steadier, he says, any place is pleasant, and he adds a line that sounds very Stoic: I wasn't born for one corner; this whole world is my homeland.
The change he's after isn't scenery. It's a habit, a judgment, a way of meeting the morning. Those come with you to the beach and to the office, and they're the only luggage worth repacking.

how: People who follow Seneca's advice often look for the habit behind a restless wish to be elsewhere, and work on that habit where they already are.

games.q: the restless traveler — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca tells Lucilius never to travel
once the soul is steadier, he says, any place is pleasant.
Seneca passes on a saying of Socrates about travel
why are you surprised, when you take yourself along?
Seneca called the whole world his homeland
I wasn't born for one corner.

games.q: you've moved cities twice and the same restlessness keeps following you. what does the twenty-eighth letter suggest?
o: try a third city, farther away.
change your soul, not your sky.
games.why: Seneca says the cause travels with you; the change has to be in the person, after which any place will do.

practice: Think of something you've hoped a change of place would fix: a new job, a move, a trip, a different chair. Ask what habit sits underneath it, rushing, comparing, never saying no, and name it in a few words.
Then picture tomorrow morning in the same room you always wake up in, with that habit just slightly different.

wordCard.voice: Socrates. His reply, passed on by Seneca: why are you surprised, when you take yourself along? Change the soul, not the sky. Today's word.
